howItWorks: Authority: the simulation owns intent (direction / speed, the cut gate, pursuit); TURN-1.2 resolves locomotion, unchanged; the resolver decides when, which foot, which boot region, which contact tick and the launch; BallWorld owns the ball from that tick on. No tether: the dribble code never writes the ball's state — it sets collider frames and schedules one launch per touch through the kernel's validated schedule().

The touch is a bounded adjustment of the free leg's swing on top of TURN-1.2's pose: a swing time-warp (the boot meets the ball at an earlier point of its own path, at a controlled speed), a bounded offset, a boot-region rotation (yaw carried by the hip), a follow-through hold, pinned to zero at touchdown — the plant never moves (0 mm over 26,076 adjusted ticks).

Candidates come from real foot opportunities in TURN-1.2's own prediction (contact tick × path phase × region × contact elevation); each must pass reach, closing speed, the approach and follow-through checks, the launch solve against the next feasible window (exact BallWorld refinement), and must not send the ball into the other leg.
Touch distance scales with speed (aimed separation 0.7 m at JOG → 2.8 m at SPRINT, longest interval 1.4 → 2.9 s); minimum intervals stop rapid fire; one deliberate touch per swing.

Foot selection: both feet's opportunities compete; cost includes the preferred / weak foot (weak-foot rating), region, reach and continuity with the window the last launch aimed at; the weak foot also raises the execution error.
Execution error (seeded, keyed per touch): σ from Dribbling 0.5 / Ball Control 0.3 / Agility 0.2, weak foot, boot region, speed and turn (Balance); Reactions set the reaction time; Agility the reach.

Cuts: a requested change of more than 8° is held until a touch can take the ball into it (at most the speed's longest touch interval + 0.3 s, then the body turns without it); staged cuts and set-up touches; the carrier's pursuit bends the run toward where the free ball will be — the ball is never corrected.
Control state is a classification only (CONTROLLED / LOOSE / CONTESTED).
visualDefects: Touch-family monotony: almost every touch is a FRONT (toe) push — 75 of 75 at JOG, 45 of 45 at RUN; inside / outside / laces appear only in cuts. At gameplay scale the rhythm reads well, close up the touches look alike.

Failed cuts end in a firm recovery push: when no touch can take the ball into the cut, the swing that meets it pushes it 9–10 m/s straight on while the body turns (k07); the cut also starts late (about 1.2 s after the request) because the player must first reach a ball he pushed 1–1.5 m ahead.
SPRINT knock-ons look like chasing a loose ball: 2.5 s between touches, the ball 2–3 m ahead; at the 1× camera player and ball are small, so contacts read only through the ball's change of speed.
systemDefects: Cut reliability (the stop-condition gap): turns taken with the ball, 8 seeds — 45° 5/8, 60° 5/8, 60° left 3/8, 90° 1/8, 90° left 2/8, 90° jog 2/8, 135° 0/8, 180° 0/8. Cause: a contact early in the swing has a fast follow-through (the time-warp must catch up to TURN-1.2's unchanged plant), so only a firm launch clears it without a second contact — the soft redirecting touch a cut needs is often infeasible. Tried tonight, measured, kept or rejected: interval consistency, gate on user changes only, speed-dependent hold, blockers, partial / staged cuts, set-up touches, pursuit on/off.

CPU: 496.6 ms per simulated second for one dribbler (Apple M4, one thread) — locomotion 28.1, ball 2.8, resolver 465.7 (predictions 270.1, launch solve 117.9); 2.01× real time on average, slower than real time in the worst cases (135°: 0.53×).

Foot preference is weak and the kernel can fail closed: the right-footed elite player makes only 31–59 % of RUN / FAST touches with his right foot (continuity with the aimed window outweighs preference); the ball kernel throws on a leg–ball–turf pinch (0 in the final 160 runs, seen during development — the run ends as a recorded fault); Node vs Chrome replay differs in 2 / 20 scenarios (ball kernel, 1e-17 level).
nextStep: DRIBBLE-1.1 — a soft-touch follow-through: after the contact tick, let the touching swing decelerate / lift around the ball and re-converge to TURN-1.2's unchanged plant (instead of the time-warp's catch-up), add it to the follow-through model, and re-run the cut matrix with the taken-with-the-ball metric (target 45–60° ≥ 7/8, 90° ≥ 5/8); in the same pass, share one locomotion prediction per input change between planning, clearance and the post-cut branches to cut the resolver's CPU.

determinismNote: The cross-engine differences start at the last bits: REV180_SPRINT in the ball's state inside the ball kernel (~6e-15 at 3.26 s), CURVE_JOG in the player's heading ψ (4.4e-16 at 2.25 s — locomotion / intent math), while the other state is still identical; a sample of common Math functions gives identical results in both engines, so the difference is in a transcendental for specific inputs between V8 versions. Same-engine replay is exact.
cpuNote: The ball kernel and TURN-1.2 are cheap (≈ 31 ms per simulated second together); the resolver's lookahead (TURN-1.2 clones for the locomotion prediction and post-cut branches) dominates. Only the ball carrier runs the resolver, so match scale means one resolver plus 22 locomotion bodies — viable for development now, with ~5× to gain before match budgets.
